video_caption: The video segment displays three distinct presentation slides with a consistent colorful border. The first slide, shown from 0:05, is titled "NEUROPHYSIOLOGY" and states the objective: "Explain the clinical significance of drugs that mimic or inhibit parasympathetic or sympathetic effects." It features a gray book cover for "Anatomy and Physiology" and the OpenStax logo. At 0:08, the slide transitions to "CLASSIFICATION OF DRUGS," presenting a diagram that illustrates "Before Drug" (natural substance binding to receptor for normal cellular activity), "Agonist Drug" (agonist drug binding to receptor for enhanced cellular activity), and "Antagonist Drug" (antagonist drug blocking the receptor, leading to blocked cellular activity). This slide includes a creative commons attribution at the bottom. The final slide, appearing at 0:26, is titled "NICOTINIC AGONISTS." It shows the chemical structure of Nicotine and explains that it "Stimulates both sympathetic and parasympathetic postganglionic fibers leading to mostly conflicting signals that cancel. However, lack of dual innervation of blood vessels leads to increased blood pressure." Below this text is an image of a field of green plants, likely tobacco, with a building in the distance, also accompanied by a creative commons attribution. Throughout the segment, an unseen speaker provides narration corresponding to the slide content.

The video segment presents a static educational slide with a white background framed by a colorful border of green, yellow, orange, and red strips at the top and bottom. The title "NICOTINIC AGONISTS" is displayed in green text at the top left. A block of black text next to the title reads: "Stimulates both sympathetic and parasympathetic postganglionic fibers leading to mostly conflicting signals that cancel. However, lack of dual innervation of blood vessels leads to increased blood pressure." Below this descriptive text, the chemical structure of "Nicotine" is shown, featuring a pyridine ring attached to a pyrrolidine ring, with the label "Nicotine" underneath. On the right side of the slide, a photograph depicts a large, verdant field of green leafy plants, likely tobacco plants, extending towards the horizon under a light blue sky, with a small building and some trees visible in the distance. Small text at the bottom right provides image attribution: "By Kotoviski (Self-published work by Kotoviski) [GFDL (http://www.gnu.org/copyleft/fdl.html), CC-BY-SA-3.0 (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/) or CC BY 2.5 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5)], via Wikimedia Commons". The slide remains unchanged throughout the duration of the segment.

The video segment displays a presentation slide titled "SYMPATHOMIMETIC DRUGS" in green text at the top. On the left side, there is a chemical structure diagram labeled "Phenylephrine," depicting a benzene ring with a hydroxyl group attached to one carbon and a side chain containing another hydroxyl group and a methylamino group. Below the chemical structure, a descriptive paragraph explains, "The sympathetic system causes pupillary dilation when norepinephrine binds to an adrenergic receptor in the radial fibers of the iris smooth muscle. Phenylephrine mimics this action by binding to the same receptor when drops are applied onto the surface of the eye in a doctor's office. (credit: Corey Theiss)." To the right, a close-up photograph of a human eye shows a significantly dilated pupil, appearing almost entirely black and much larger than the visible light green iris. The slide has a white background with colorful vertical and horizontal border stripes in green, yellow, orange, and blue, and an "openstax" logo is present in the top right corner.

This video segment displays a single slide titled "SYMPATHOMIMETIC DRUGS" in green text at the top left. In the top right corner, the "openstax" logo is visible. The slide's background is white with a colorful border of green, yellow, orange, and blue strips. On the left side of the slide, there's a chemical structure labeled "Phenylephrine" in black text below it. This structure shows a benzene ring with hydroxyl (HO) group attached, connected to a chain containing another hydroxyl (OH) group and a secondary amine (NH) group. Below this, a paragraph of text explains that "The sympathetic system causes pupillary dilation when norepinephrine binds to an adrenergic receptor in the radial fibers of the iris smooth muscle. Phenylephrine mimics this action by binding to the same receptor when drops are applied onto the surface of the eye in a doctor's office. (credit: Corey Theiss)". To the right of the text and chemical structure, a close-up photograph of a human eye with a dilated pupil is featured. The iris appears light green/hazel, and the pupil is very large and dark, reflecting a small light source.

The video segment displays a slide titled "SYMPATHOLYTIC DRUGS" in green text against a white background with colorful abstract borders. In the top right corner, the "openstax" logo is visible. On the left side, the chemical structure of "Propranolol (beta-blocker)" is shown. In the center, a pink and red capsule pill with the text "MYLAN 6180" is displayed. To the right, a diagram illustrates the autonomic nervous system's control over the heart, featuring a human brain, spinal cord, and heart. Arrows from the brain are labeled "The vagus nerve (parasympathetic) decreases heart rate," while arrows from the spinal cord are labeled "Sympathetic cardiac nerves increases heart rate and force of contraction." At the bottom left, a list states "Prescribed for:" followed by medical conditions: "High blood pressure," "Irregular heart rhythm (arrhythmia)," "Heart failure," "Chest pain (angina)," and "Heart attacks." The overall visual content educates about sympatholytic drugs and their applications.

The video segment displays a slide titled "SYMPATHOLYTIC DRUGS" in green text at the top left, with the OpenStax logo in the top right. On the left, a chemical structure is shown, labeled "Propranolol (beta-blocker)." Below this, a pink and orange pharmaceutical capsule is pictured, embossed with "MYLAN 6180." Further down, a list details the conditions for which it is prescribed: "High blood pressure," "Irregular heart rhythm (arrhythmia)," "Heart failure," "Chest pain (angina)," and "Heart attacks." On the right side of the slide, a diagram illustrates the innervation of the heart by the autonomic nervous system. The brain is shown at the top, with text indicating "The vagus nerve (parasympathetic) decreases heart rate" with an arrow pointing from the brainstem to the heart. Below this, "Sympathetic cardiac nerves increase heart rate and force of contraction" is written, with lines originating from the spinal cord region extending to various parts of the heart, labeled T1-T4. The background of the slide is white, framed by a colorful border of vertical stripes in green, yellow, orange, and blue.

The video begins with a slide titled "SYMPATHOLYTIC DRUGS" (English), featuring the chemical structure of "Propranolol (beta-blocker)" (English) next to a pink and red capsule labeled "MYLAN 6180" (English). Below this, a bulleted list indicates that it's "Prescribed for: High blood pressure, Irregular heart rhythm (arrhythmia), Heart failure, Chest pain (angina), Heart attacks" (English). On the right side of the slide, an anatomical diagram illustrates the brain, spinal cord, and heart, showing pathways of "The vagus nerve (parasympathetic) decreases heart rate" (English) and "Sympathetic cardiac nerves increases heart rate and force of contraction" (English) connecting to the heart. This slide transitions at 0:10 to a new slide titled "PARASYMPATHOMIMETIC DRUGS" (English), which presents the chemical structures of "Pilocarpine" (English) and "Muscarine" (English), along with a photograph of a red and white spotted mushroom labeled "Amanita muscaria" (English), and a credit for the image. Both slides feature an "openstax™" (English) logo in the top right corner and a vibrant, striped border on the left and right edges.

The video displays a static educational slide titled "PARASYMPATHOMIMETIC DRUGS" in green text at the top, with the "openstax" logo and colorful bars in the top right and left corners, respectively. On the left side of the slide, two chemical structures are shown. The top structure is labeled "Pilocarpine," and the bottom structure is labeled "Muscarine." On the right side of the slide, there is a close-up photograph of two red mushrooms with white spots, typical of the *Amanita muscaria* species, growing in green grass and brown soil. Below the mushrooms, the text "Amanita muscaria" is visible. A small credit line is present at the bottom left corner of the slide, stating: "Credit: By Mgrzen71 (GFDL, http://www.gnu.org/copyleft/fdl.html) or CC BY-SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)], from Wikimedia Commons." The slide remains unchanged throughout the segment.

The video segment displays a slide titled "PARASYMPATHOMIMETIC DRUGS" in green text against a white background with a colorful border composed of vertical stripes in green, yellow, blue, and orange. In the top right corner, the "openstax™" logo is visible. The slide features two chemical structures and one image. In the top left, the chemical structure for "Pilocarpine" is shown, consisting of a bicyclic ring system with an oxygen and a nitrogen atom, and several methyl and ethyl groups. Below it, the chemical structure for "Muscarine" is presented, which is a bicyclic molecule with an oxygen atom in one ring and a positively charged nitrogen atom with three methyl groups attached in another part of the molecule. To the right of the chemical structures, there is a photograph of two vibrant red mushrooms with white flecks on their caps, emerging from green grass and brown earth. This image is labeled "Amanita muscaria". At the bottom of the slide, a credit reads: "Credit: By Mrgreen71 (GFDL (http://www.gnu.org/copyleft/fdl.html) or CC BY-SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)], from Wikimedia Commons".

The video displays two distinct slides, each featuring chemical structures and a corresponding image, framed by a colorful border of green, yellow, blue, orange, and red stripes, with an "openstax" logo in the top right corner. The first slide, visible from 00:03 to 00:57, is titled "PARASYMPATHOMIMETIC DRUGS" in green text. On the left, it shows the chemical structures of "Pilocarpine" and "Muscarine." On the right, a close-up photograph of a bright red mushroom with white flecks on its cap, labeled "Amanita muscaria," is embedded in green grass and dried leaves. The speaker discusses how Muscarine was initially thought to be the cause of toxicity from the Amanita muscaria mushroom. The second slide, appearing at 00:58, is titled "ANTICHOLINERGIC DRUGS" in green text. On the left, it presents the chemical structure of "Atropine." On the right, a photograph shows a plant with dark green leaves, small purple bell-shaped flowers, and shiny black berries, identified as "Atropa Belladonna Deadly Nightshade Plant." Both slides include credit text at the bottom left.

The video displays a static slide featuring a white background with a vibrant, multi-colored border of orange, green, blue, and yellow stripes on all four sides. At the top left, the title "ANTICHOLINERGIC DRUGS" is written in bold, green, uppercase letters. In the top right corner, the "openstax" logo appears in black text, accompanied by four stacked horizontal bars in shades of green, gray, and red. The left side of the slide presents a chemical structure labeled "Atropine" below it, depicting a complex organic molecule. On the right, a photograph shows a lush green plant with several purple, bell-shaped flowers and numerous glossy black berries. Below this image, the text "Atropa Belladonna" and "Deadly Nightshade Plant" is displayed. A male voice provides a narration, explaining that a muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist, such as atropine (derived from the Atropa Belladonna plant), would be classified as a parasympatholytic drug, decreasing parasympathetic responses.

The video displays a presentation slide with the title "ANTICHOLINERGIC DRUGS" in green text at the top left and an "openstax™" logo at the top right. The main content is split into two sections. On the left, there is a chemical structure labeled "Atropine," depicting a complex organic molecule with a nitrogen-containing ring system, an ester group, a hydroxyl group, and a benzene ring. On the right, a photograph shows a lush green plant with several dark purple, almost black, berries and some small purple flowers, growing in what appears to be a natural outdoor setting with other greenery in the background. Below this image, two lines of text read "Atropa Belladonna" and "Deadly Nightshade Plant," identifying the plant. The entire slide has a white background with a colorful border composed of vertical and horizontal blocks of orange, blue, green, and yellow on the left, right, and bottom edges.

The video opens with a slide titled "ANTICHOLINERGIC DRUGS" in green text at the top left, with the "openstax™" logo at the top right. On the left side of the slide is a chemical structure labeled "Atropine," which features a complex ring system with an attached ester group, including a benzene ring and a hydroxyl group. To the right of the chemical structure, there's a photograph of a plant identified as "Atropa Belladonna Deadly Nightshade Plant." This plant has green leaves, dark purple-black berries, and some small purple bell-shaped flowers. The background of the slide is white, framed by colorful vertical stripes on the left and horizontal stripes at the bottom. At 0:19, the slide transitions to a "RESOURCES" slide, also with a white background and colored stripes. This new slide displays the "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike" icon and lists two bullet points for attribution: "Slides were modified from: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, OpenStax: © Rice University under a CC-BY 4.0 International license; and may be reproduced or modified but must be attributed to OpenStax, Rice University and any changes must be noted," and "By Dolleyj - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=32459362." The audio discusses Atropine's effects, mentioning its ability to increase heart rate and its clinical use as a medication.
